sections.h2: Who values and bills property tax in Charlotte?
sections.html:
Mecklenburg County's Office of Tax Administration values every parcel in Charlotte and collects the county's tax, and the City of Charlotte's own property tax rides on the same bill. The county's rate page says a total bill includes a municipal tax from Charlotte or one of the six county towns, plus county and municipal solid waste fees where they apply. Payments go to the City-County Tax Collector.

The office's own description covers valuing parcels, collecting ad valorem and business gross receipts taxes, and running relief programs. Appeals, relief applications and the revaluation all run through the county. City Council's part is the city rate, which it sets in its yearly budget.

Payment options on the county page include a toll-free card line at 1-800-994-1026 that answers day and night, mailed checks to Charlotte post office boxes, bank eCheck payments, and counter service during weekday office hours. A payment with no 24-digit bill number in the account box is rejected and returned. Cards carry a vendor fee of $3.95 on Visa or Mastercard debit and 2.35 percent (minimum $1.95) on other cards, while eChecks carry none. A bank-initiated payment can take up to four business days to post.

sections.h2: What are the Charlotte property tax rates and key dates?
sections.html:
The Mecklenburg County rate is 49.27 cents on each $100 of value, and the county adopted its FY2027 budget on June 2, 2026 with that rate unchanged. The city rate comes on top of it for property inside Charlotte, and the figure for a given year appears on your bill and in the city budget. The table lists the items that matter most to a seller.

sections.h2: What is the route for contesting a Charlotte tax value?
sections.html:
You file a Formal Appeal Form with the county Office of Tax Administration, and the board of equalization and review hears it. In a normal year the deadline is the board's adjournment date, which was May 4, 2026 for the most recent cycle. The only exception is for owners who receive a notice of value change, who may file by the later of adjournment or the last date to appeal on the notice.

  • File by email to the county's appeals address, by mail to Mecklenburg County BER Real Property Appeals, P.O. Box 31127, Charlotte, NC 28231, or in person at 3205 Freedom Dr, Suite 3500, Charlotte, NC 28208.
  • Back-up documents must arrive with the form or within 45 days of filing it. Anyone other than you or an attorney who speaks for you needs a signed power of attorney.
  • Expect the hearing notice roughly a month before your slot, and send any request to reschedule in writing within ten days of that notice.
  • The board's ruling comes by mail within a month of the hearing. If you disagree, the Property Tax Commission in Raleigh takes the next appeal, and you have 30 days to file it.

The burden sits with the owner, who must show the tax value substantially exceeds market value. No revaluation-year appeal can be filed before notices of value go out, and the county expects the notices and refreshed online records in early 2027.

Between revaluations, the county keeps the prior value unless a ground in G.S. 105-287(a) applies. The county lists clerical or arithmetic mistakes, a misapplied schedule of values, physical changes to the land or buildings, and a change in legal use.

sections.h2: Does Charlotte offer property tax relief for homeowners?
sections.html:
Yes. Mecklenburg County runs the state homestead programs from its tax relief page, and its FY2027 budget carries $3.5 million for the county's HOMES program, described as relief for qualifying homeowners. A Charlotte owner applies to the county for all of them, and the tax office contact page lists a mailbox for real estate relief questions.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: removes half of a home's appraised value, or $25,000 if that is more, for owners aged 65 and up or permanently and totally disabled whose income stays within the cap (NCDOR printed $38,800 for 2026).
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: removes $45,000 of appraised value through Form NCDVA-9, whatever the owner's age or income.
  • Circuit breaker: defers the part of the bill above 4 or 5 percent of income, depending on where income falls between the cap and $58,200. The deferred amount is a lien and, on a transfer, comes due together with the prior three years.

The county page defines income broadly, counting every source except family gifts and inheritances. File Form AV-9 with the county, which has to take applications up to June 1 ahead of the tax year.

sections.h2: Who settles the Charlotte tax bill when a house sells?
sections.html:
Any balance gets cleared from sale proceeds at closing, because the debt rides with the parcel. The lien arises on January 1, so a house sold in March already owes that year's tax even though the September 1 due date has not arrived. Treat that year's amount as a payoff line.

After January 5 a bill starts accruing interest, 2 percent for the rest of January and three-fourths of a percent per month after that. Prolonged nonpayment lets the county file a court action modeled on mortgage foreclosure, with an auction sale. An owner can redeem ahead of confirmation by paying everything owed. The tax office site also hosts a Delinquent Taxpayer Lists page.

On the deed side, the seller (transferor) pays North Carolina's excise tax to the Mecklenburg County register of deeds before the deed is recorded. Your closing attorney can confirm the stamps and filing charges that will show on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: What does Charlotte look like for a house seller?
sections.html:
Census Bureau figures show Charlotte at 964,784 people for July 1, 2025, a 10.3 percent rise over the 2020 base. The land area is 308.29 square miles, with 2,836.9 residents per square mile in 2020. Owners occupy 51.0 percent of homes, which leaves renters with almost half.

Over 2020-2024 the typical owned home was valued at $385,700, gross rent at a median of $1,612 and household income at a median of $82,068. Roughly 48.0 percent of adults over 25 hold at least a bachelor's degree, and workers average a 24.7-minute trip to work. The city's FY2027 budget also counts on a new voter-approved sales tax for mobility.

The 2027 values will draw on four years of sales since 2023. A seller listing in early 2027 should watch for the notice mailing, since the new assessment shapes later tax bills and a buyer may ask about it.

faqs.q: What is the property tax rate in Charlotte?
faqs.a: The county levy is 49.27 cents on each $100 of value, and the FY2027 budget left it alone. Charlotte adds its own city rate to that for property inside the city, set by City Council each year. Your bill shows both, along with any solid waste fee.

faqs.q: When is the next Charlotte revaluation?
faqs.a: The next one lands in 2027. Mecklenburg County moved to a four-year cycle, and the previous revaluation was 2023. Notices and updated online records are expected in early 2027, and the county's page invites an informal review request within 30 days of the notice date.

faqs.q: How do I pay a Charlotte property tax bill?
faqs.a: Use the card line at 1-800-994-1026, send an eCheck, mail a check to the City-County Tax Collector, or visit during weekday hours. Whatever you choose, include the 24-digit bill number, since a payment without it is returned. Cards bring a vendor fee.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Charlotte property value after the deadline?
faqs.a: Not for the 2026 cycle. Requests had to be in by May 4, 2026, unless a notice of value change gave you a later last date. The next broad opening follows the 2027 revaluation notices.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid Charlotte property tax when I sell?
faqs.a: It comes out of your proceeds at closing, with interest added if the bill is past January 5. The lien has attached to the parcel since January 1 of the tax year. Get the balance from the Mecklenburg Office of Tax Administration before you sign a contract.
